def: Any assisted reproduction technique (artificial insemination, in vitro fertilization) used to control the genetics and productivity of animals.
A Brazilian brand of creamy soy-based vegan cheese, inspired by ricotta.
The act of removing an animal from a situation of exploitation, abandonment or risk, usually followed by rehabilitation or adoption.
Recognition of a being's value that guides treatment consistent with its dignity or interests.
com: Extending respect to a being implies recognizing its interests as morally relevant, regardless of its usefulness or its similarity to humans.

def: Forced confrontation between animals (roosters, dogs) for entertainment and betting, usually illegal.
Risks of suffering on an astronomical scale ("s-risks"), a concept tied to concern about massive future suffering, including that of animals.
Existential risks, capable of extinguishing sentient life or its future potential.
Practices of sacrifice or ritual use, a sensitive topic at the intersection of ethics and religion.
A spectacle in which horses or bulls are ridden or chased by competitors, involving methods that induce stressful behavior in the animal.
A tourist activity of observing (or hunting) wild animals in their habitat, with debates about its impact on welfare and conservation.
A sulfurous salt of volcanic or mineral origin, used in vegan cooking to reproduce the taste of egg in recipes.
A nonprofit institution dedicated to taking in and caring for rescued animals, with no purpose of exploitation or commercial breeding.
Solid fat extracted from animal tissues, used to make candles, soaps and some foods.
A textile fiber produced by silkworm larvae, whose traditional extraction usually involves killing the larvae inside the cocoon.
Guaranteed regular and permanent access to food of sufficient quality for a healthy life, a topic connected to food justice.
Deliberate human choice of desired genetic traits in animals through controlled breeding.
Small reproductive structures of plants, used as food, oil or as the base of plant-based cheeses.
The capacity to feel, to have positive or negative subjective experiences such as pain, pleasure and fear.
com: For sentientism, it is sentience, and not species, intelligence or a being's usefulness to others, that is the only morally relevant criterion for determining who deserves consideration.

termo: Sentience in AI and digital systems
def: The debate over whether artificial systems could develop subjective experience and, if so, deserve moral consideration.
com: A consistent sentientist perspective would require extending moral consideration to these systems once there is sufficient evidence of sentience, regardless of their biological or artificial origin.
pt: Senciência em IA e sistemas digitais

def: A variant of the previous discussion applied to artificial physical bodies; a frontier question in machine ethics.
com: (see the note under Sentience in AI and digital systems)

def: The speculative extension of the moral circle to hypothetical sentient life forms beyond Earth.
com: From a sentientist standpoint, a being's cosmic origin is morally irrelevant: what matters is solely its capacity to suffer or feel pleasure.

def: A position that takes sentience, not species, as the criterion of moral inclusion; also called sentiocentrism.
com: It is the criterion adopted, explicitly or implicitly, in most of the critical remarks in this dictionary.

def: A proposal for political and social organization guided by the interests of all sentient beings.
com: It represents the broadest institutional and political application of sentientism, proposing to extend representation and political participation, today restricted to humans, to all beings capable of having interests.

def: Any being capable of having subjective experiences, positive or negative.
com: It is this category, and not that of "human being" or "intelligent being", that for sentientism correctly delimits the circle of those who deserve moral consideration.

def: Any organism that exhibits biological processes such as metabolism, growth and reproduction; a broader category than "sentient being", since it also includes plants and microorganisms. Not every living being is sentient.
com: This distinction is central to sentientism, which grants direct moral consideration only to beings capable of feeling, which sets it apart from biocentric currents that extend moral value to every form of life.

def: A network of specialized cells (neurons) that allows an organism to process stimuli and coordinate responses; the proposed physiological basis for the capacity to feel.
com: The absence of a nervous system of the known kind in certain species should not, by itself, be taken as proof of the absence of sentience, given how limited scientific knowledge on the subject still is.

def: The part of the nervous system made up of the brain and spinal cord, sometimes used as a criterion for inferring the presence of sentience in a species.
com: Adopting this anatomical criterion exclusively risks underestimating the capacity to feel in species with different nervous architectures, such as octopuses and many insects.

def: A movement that values traditional, local and carefully prepared food, as opposed to fast food.
A set of political currents that advocate collective ownership or control of the means of production and the reduction of class inequalities.
com: Authors such as Ted Benton and David Nibert apply the critique of exploitation and commodification to animals.

def: A negative experience central to most justifications for moral consideration.
Pain and death that occur without human intervention (disease, predation, disasters).
A philosophical debate over whether and how humans would have an obligation to intervene to reduce suffering in nature.
A versatile legume, the basis of countless vegan products (tofu, milk, soy meat).
The degree to which a being is taken into account for its own sake in the ethical decisions of others.
com: For sentientism, a being's moral status derives solely from its capacity to feel, not from its species, intelligence or usefulness to others.

def: The current state of things.
com: Invoking it to justify maintaining practices of animal exploitation is considered by antispeciesists to be a fallacy: the fact that something is customary does not imply that it is morally right.

def: A subculture originating in hardcore punk, characterized by abstinence from alcohol, drugs and, in many cases, animal products, often associated with ethical veganism.
com: This convergence illustrates how the conscious refusal of certain kinds of consumption can become, for some adherents, a broader political and ethical extension, including the rejection of animal exploitation.

def: The condition of being a "subject-of-a-life", with one's own perspective on what happens to one (a central concept in Tom Regan, cited only as a reference).
com: Recognizing a being's subjectivity implies recognizing it as someone, and not as something, a shift in perspective central to overcoming speciesism.

def: The use of animals out of a need for direct survival, a recurring argument in debates about ethical exceptions.
The position that what matters morally is ensuring that all individuals reach a sufficient minimum threshold of well-being, prioritizing those below that threshold.
com: From this standpoint, ensuring that no animal has its well-being reduced below a minimally acceptable threshold would be morally more urgent than maximizing aggregate well-being or seeking full equality.

def: A concept from Tom Regan (cited only as a reference) designating beings with a unified psychophysical existence, memory, preferences and a well-being of their own, who deserve basic rights.
com: This concept underpins the defense of basic rights, to life and to liberty, for various nonhuman species, and not only for humans.

def: In the livestock context, an identification plate used on animals or rural properties.
A paste made from ground sesame seeds, the base ingredient of hummus.
A fermented soy-based food of Indonesian origin, rich in protein.
The view that God or the divine is the center of reality and morality.
com: Theocentric traditions vary: some see animals as created to serve humans, while others call for compassion and care toward them, as in ahimsa and tza'ar ba'alei chayim.

def: The capacity to attribute mental states to oneself and to others; studied in primates, corvids and cetaceans as an indication of cognitive complexity. Evidence of theory of mind in many species reinforces the idea that cognitive complexity is not exclusively human, undermining one of the traditional arguments of speciesism.
An umbrella term for the set of normative approaches (consequentialism, deontology, virtue ethics, care ethics and others) used to justify moral positions, including on animals.
com: How each of these theories treats, or fails to treat, animals as moral subjects is one of the main axes of comparison among them within animal ethics.

def: The practice of publicly documenting animal suffering at sites of exploitation (slaughterhouses, markets).
A food obtained by coagulating soy milk and pressing it into blocks; one of the main sources of vegan protein.
A brand of tofu-based products formulated to imitate turkey meat, associated with vegan festive meals.
A spectacle involving a confrontation between a bull and bullfighters, usually resulting in serious injury and the death of the animal.
The use of an animal's physical strength to pull loads or vehicles.
A labeling warning indicating possible cross-contamination of a product with small unintentional amounts of an ingredient (such as milk or egg).
The illegal trade in wild or domestic animals, often involving capture, transport and cruel conditions.
A gradual process of changing eating habits, usually toward reducing or eliminating animal products.
A stage of the production chain associated with stress, injuries and mortality.
A person responsible for the care of a companion animal; a term preferred by activists over "owner", because it does not imply a property relationship.
The practice of taking on continuing responsibility for the care of an animal, usually a rescued one, as an alternative to the concept of ownership.
The principle that valid moral judgments must apply equally to all relevantly similar cases, regardless of who carries them out.
com: It is the logical basis of the argument from marginal cases and of much of the antispeciesist critique: if a moral criterion holds for humans in a given situation, it must hold equally for animals in a relevantly similar situation.

def: A consequentialist strand that seeks to maximize well-being and minimize the aggregate suffering of those affected by a decision (reference: Bentham, Singer, cited only as examples).
com: Bentham already pointed out, as early as the eighteenth century, that the relevant question about animals is not whether they can reason or talk, but whether they can suffer, a seminal formulation of sentientism.

def: The version of utilitarianism that seeks to maximize the total aggregate sum of well-being of all those affected by a decision, without giving additional weight to those who are worse off.
com: It differs from negative utilitarianism in holding that positive experiences can, in principle, compensate for suffering.

def: A variant of utilitarianism whose goal is to minimize the total aggregate of suffering, holding that no amount of positive well-being can compensate for it. This variant tends to give stronger moral priority to eliminating animal suffering than to promoting positive experiences, which brings it closer to more urgent positions within the animal liberation movement.
The value attributed to something because of its usefulness for another end, and not for its own sake.
com: Treating animals exclusively as bearers of instrumental value, as resources, is the core of the abolitionist and antispeciesist critique of their status as property.

def: The value a being has in itself, regardless of its usefulness to others; also called inherent value.
com: It is the central concept of animal rights theories, which hold that every subject-of-a-life has intrinsic value, incompatible with being treated as a mere resource.

def: A traditional Brazilian practice in which two cowboys on horseback chase a bull and bring it down by the tail, causing physical injuries to the animal.
The use of vegan or plant-based imagery by brands or companies with no real commitment to the animal cause.
com: It is criticized for diluting the ethical meaning of veganism, reducing it to a market trend detached from the moral consideration for animals that originally motivates it.

def: A philosophy and practice that seeks to exclude, as far as possible and practicable, all forms of animal exploitation.
A strand that emphasizes ending animals' status as property as its central axis, critical of welfarism.
A strand that links veganism with a critique of patriarchal structures (connected to ecofeminism).
A strand that connects the animal cause to other forms of oppression (race, class, gender).
A strand aimed at the economic and cultural accessibility of veganism for working-class communities.
A strand focused on results and harm reduction, prioritizing mass adoption over ideological purity.
A broad term referring to the exclusion of meat from the diet, without necessarily excluding all animal products.

A term used in Brazil as a synonym for a 100% plant-based diet (excluding meat, dairy, eggs and honey), distinct from veganism as a broader philosophy that also covers clothing, entertainment and other uses of animals.
The medical science dedicated to the prevention, diagnosis and treatment of diseases, trauma and disorders in animals.
com: Historically, because much of its practice is oriented toward animal exploitation and productivity, the field is in tension with welfare approaches and non-anthropocentric worldviews.

def: A current that discusses the moral dilemmas of veterinary practice, such as euthanasia, the use of animals in livestock farming and experimentation.
com: One of its central dilemmas is the fact that a good part of veterinary professionals work directly in the service of animal exploitation systems, which creates conflict between the duty of care and the economic function of the work.

def: Systematic distortions of judgment that affect how animal suffering is perceived. Biases such as cognitive dissonance and conformity bias help explain why widely shared beliefs about the moral value of animals do not always translate into consistent behavior.
An essential nutrient produced by microorganisms, not reliably present in plant sources, whose supplementation is usually recommended in vegan diets.
Meat from calves slaughtered while still young, usually raised in conditions of extreme confinement (veal crate).
Experimentation on live animals, a historically loaded term used by antivivisection movements.

Moral discrimination among different nonhuman species, privileging some (e.g. dogs, dolphins) over others (e.g. insects, fish) without a morally relevant justification. It is pointed out by sentientists as a "second-degree" form of speciesism: even among those who already reject human superiority, aesthetic preferences or preferences based on similarity end up recreating morally arbitrary hierarchies among nonhuman species.
The transplantation of organs or tissues between different species (e.g. from pigs to humans), raising ethical questions about the use of animals as "organ banks".
A film that forms on the surface of heated soy milk, used as food in Asian cuisine.

A psychological state of familiarity and low risk that tends to resist change. In the context of animal consumption, it is often cited as one of the main psychological obstacles to adopting habits more aligned with the equal consideration of interests across species.
The practice of sexual activity between humans and animals; a crime and a serious form of animal abuse.
The branch of biology dedicated to the scientific study of animals.
com: Like ethology, zoology has helped dismantle traditional hierarchies among species by revealing the biological and behavioral complexity of organisms once considered "inferior".

def: An institution that keeps wild animals in captivity for display, education or research; a central target of criticism by the animal liberation movement.
A disease transmissible between animals and humans, a topic relevant to debates on industrial livestock farming and public health.
Pleasure derived from inflicting suffering or death on animals; a form of cruelty associated with behavioral disorders.

A science applied to the breeding and management of animals for production, historically oriented toward productivity and economic yield. Because it defines animals primarily as productive resources, zootechnics is often pointed to by abolitionist currents as a structurally speciesist discipline, even when it incorporates welfare parameters.
